strengths: Timely and relevant problem: enabling drag-based editing with modern DiT/flow-matching backbones (FLUX) is a natural and underexplored direction, and the paper is among the first to seriously attempt it.

The feature-granularity analysis (UNet bottleneck vs. DiT features, Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2, Appendix Figs. 7-8) provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for why point-based supervision transfers poorly to DiTs.

The ablation study (Table 3, Fig. 6) includes a point-based FLUX baseline, so the core claim that region-level supervision outperforms point-level supervision on the same backbone is supported by evidence, not just by comparison against SD-based methods.
The proposed ReD Bench provides region-level annotations with task tags (relocation/deformation/rotation), which could be a useful community resource.
The paper is generally well organized and the methodology (progressive affine mask propagation, hard background constraints, adapter-enhanced inversion) is described with enough detail to follow.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness is a serious concern. The authors modify the MD2 metric on DragBench-DR by 'replacing point-based annotations with an automatic centroid-based formulation' (Appendix E.2, G.2), i.e., they change the evaluation protocol of an existing benchmark in a way that plausibly favors their own region-centroid-based method, while all baselines were designed under the original protocol. Results under the unmodified metric are not reported.

The method depends on a proprietary MLLM (GPT-5, OpenAI 2025) at inference time for intent inference and prompt generation, which harms reproducibility and raises fairness questions: it is unclear whether baselines received the same text prompts/intent labels, and the contribution of this MLLM component is not ablated.

Many gains likely stem from the stronger base model rather than the method. Baselines run on SD-family backbones while DragFlow uses FLUX.1-dev; the '#Params (M)' column (0 for DragFlow) is misleading since it hides reliance on a 12B-parameter backbone, and no compute/runtime comparison is provided despite 70 optimization iterations at the 7th denoising step.

Limited novelty of individual components: region/affine supervision echoes RotationDrag and RegionDrag, gradient-mask hard constraints resemble Blended Latent Diffusion / inpainting-style latent blending, and KV injection plus personalization adapters (IP-Adapter, InstantCharacter) are standard techniques recombined rather than a new mechanism.

The self-curated ReD Bench contains only 120 images and no human evaluation is conducted anywhere; all metrics are LPIPS-based proxies, which are known to be weak indicators of perceptual editing quality, and IFbg trivially equals 1.000 for copy-paste methods like RegionDrag.

Improvements on DragBench-DR are modest (e.g., MD2 5.93 vs. GoodDrag's 6.91), and the paper's own limitation section admits detail loss from CFG-distilled inversion drift, which the adapter trick only partially mitigates.

The paper claims 'first framework' and 'new state-of-the-art' repeatedly, but given the modified metrics, MLLM-assisted inputs, and backbone advantage, these claims are stronger than the evidence; several loose writing issues (e.g., 'Evalutaion', inconsistent benchmark naming 'ReD Bench'/'Regional-based Dragging') further reduce polish.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated contribution: the paper is the first to systematically bring drag-based editing to DiT/FLUX backbones, and the analysis in Sec. 3.1 (UNet vs. DiT feature granularity, CFG-distillation-induced inversion drift) provides a plausible and well-illustrated explanation for why prior point-based objectives transfer poorly.

The three technical components (region-level affine supervision with progressive mask propagation, hard gradient-mask background constraints replacing soft background losses, and adapter-enhanced inversion) are coherent, well-motivated, and each is validated in a progressive ablation (Tab. 3, Fig. 6) showing measurable gains in both MD and IF metrics.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against nine representative baselines spanning optimization-, fine-tuning-, and copy-paste-based paradigms on two benchmarks (DragBench-DR and the new ReD Bench), plus extensive qualitative comparisons across diverse, challenging scenarios (Figs. 5, 12, 13).

Introduction of ReD Bench with region-level annotations, task tags (relocation/deformation/rotation), anchors, and point-to-region alignment fills a genuine gap in evaluation resources for region-based dragging; the appendix provides detailed metric definitions, prompts, and data samples.

The ablation includes a point-based FLUX variant as a baseline, which partially controls for the stronger backbone and supports the claim that region-level supervision (not just the FLUX prior) drives the improvement.
weaknesses: Fairness of headline comparisons is a concern: in Tab. 2, DragFlow (built on the 12B FLUX.1-dev model) is compared against baselines built on much weaker SD backbones, so part of the reported gain likely comes from the base model rather than the method. Only the ablation (Tab. 3) controls for this, and there is no direct comparison against a strong DiT-based point-dragging method in the main table (the adapted 'Point-based FLUX Dragger' appears only qualitatively).

Several metrics appear structurally favorable to the method: IF_bg is computed with the authors' own hard gradient mask B, which by construction freezes the background, making near-ceiling scores (0.992 on ReD Bench) almost guaranteed; likewise IF_s2t compares the output against the authors' own affine-transformed source, which directly matches their training objective. Baselines without hard constraints or affine formulations are disadvantaged. The centroid-based modification of MD2, made by the authors themselves, should be validated against the original protocol.

Heavy dependence on external components reduces reproducibility and self-containedness: the pipeline requires GPT-5 as an MLLM for intent classification and prompt generation (a closed, costly API), a pretrained InstantCharacter adapter, and FireFlow inversion. No inference cost/runtime comparison with baselines is reported despite the extra reconstruction branch and 70 latent-optimization iterations, which appear expensive.

ReD Bench is small (120 images) and curated by the authors with masks generated by the authors' own automatic masker, raising the possibility of benchmark bias toward the proposed method; no user study or perceptual evaluation supplements the LPIPS-based metrics, which are known to be imperfect for judging edit realism and deformation artifacts.

Novelty of individual components is moderate when viewed in isolation: region/affine-style supervision, background hard constraints (cf. blended latent diffusion), and adapter-based identity injection are each combinations of existing ideas; the contribution rests mainly on their integration for DiTs and the empirical analysis, which is thin on quantitative feature-analysis evidence (Sec. 3.1 relies largely on qualitative PCA visualizations in the appendix).

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'setting a new state-of-the-art in drag-based image editing' rests on benchmarks/metrics the authors themselves designed or modified, and the limitation that CFG-distilled inversion still degrades detail in complex images is acknowledged but only anecdotally addressed.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the paper provides the first systematic study of drag-based editing on DiT/flow-matching backbones (FLUX), and the analysis of UNet vs. DiT feature granularity (Fig. 2, Fig. 7-9) is a genuinely useful contribution that explains why point-based supervision transfers poorly.

The region-level affine supervision with progressive mask propagation is a clean, principled replacement for point supervision + point tracking, and the hard background constraint (Eq. 4) and adapter-enhanced inversion are pragmatic and effective solutions to real issues (inversion drift in CFG-distilled models, evidenced quantitatively in Tab. 1).

Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: comparisons against 9 recent baselines on two benchmarks, component-wise ablations, an exhaustive 57-layer feature-selection ablation, an MLLM prompt ablation (Tab. 5), backbone generalization to SD3.5 (Tab. 7), IP-Adapter vs. LoRA (Tab. 8), runtime/memory comparison (Tab. 6), and honest failure-case analysis.
Introduces a new region-based dragging benchmark (ReD Bench) with task tags, point-to-region alignment, and intent prompts, releasing code and data, which benefits future work.
Well-written and clearly organized; the qualitative results (Figs. 5, 14-16) convincingly show reduced distortion on text, statues, and fine structures compared to SD-based baselines.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is moderate: region-based inputs already exist (RegionDrag), and the affine mask propagation (Eq. 2) plus gradient masking are relatively straightforward engineering; the headline gains may stem substantially from swapping to the much stronger FLUX prior rather than from the proposed supervision design. The controlled point-vs-region comparison (Tab. 4) shows meaningful but not dramatic differences (MD1 37.02 vs 31.59).

Comparison fairness is a concern: all baselines run on Stable Diffusion while DragFlow uses a substantially larger, newer backbone; a stronger experiment would re-implement leading point-based methods (e.g., DragDiffusion/GoodDrag) directly on FLUX. The ablation (Tab. 3/4) partially addresses this but only for the authors' own point-based variant, on DragBench-DR rather than ReD Bench.

Metrics are partly self-modified: the authors redefine MD2 to be centroid-based (App. E.2) because they argue the original point-based protocol is unfair to region methods; while the reasoning is plausible, reporting both original and modified metrics (or third-party metrics/human evaluation) would strengthen credibility. There is no user study.

The MLLM component appears marginal: Tab. 5 shows Null Prompt (MD1 33.81) nearly matches GPT-5 prompts (31.59), so its contribution is small relative to the added complexity and dependency on a closed-source model (GPT-5), which hurts reproducibility.
Some metrics weakly differentiate methods (IFs2t differences of ~0.01 across many baselines), and ReD Bench is small (120 images).
High computational cost: 158.7s and 23.5GB peak memory per edit is the most expensive method compared, a significant practical limitation only partially mitigated by quantization/CPU offloading.

Minor issues: 'first framework' claims are stated strongly; several appendix references are imprecise (e.g., 'Eq. 3.2'); the affine assumption for deformation is applied to edge subregions with limited formal justification.

strengths: The paper is, to my knowledge, the first systematic attempt to bring drag-based editing to DiT/flow-matching backbones (FLUX.1-dev, SD3.5), and the motivating analysis of why point-based supervision mismatches DiT feature geometry (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2) is reasonable and clearly argued.

The three components (region-level affine supervision, gradient-mask hard constraints, adapter-enhanced inversion) are individually ablated (Tab. 3), and the quantitative ablation shows consistent gains from each component rather than only end-to-end comparisons.

The paper introduces ReD Bench with region-level instructions and task tags, and provides extensive supplementary material: layer-wise feature analysis (Fig. 9), MLLM prompt ablation (Tab. 5), runtime/memory comparison (Tab. 6), generalization to SD3.5 (Tab. 7), and IP-Adapter vs. LoRA comparison (Tab. 8).
Writing and figure quality are generally good; failure cases and input-precision limitations are honestly discussed (H.3).
weaknesses: Confounded baseline comparison: the central empirical claim of superiority is largely confounded with the backbone. All baselines in Tab. 2 are SD-based while DragFlow uses FLUX.1, a dramatically stronger prior. The paper's own narrative attributes prior methods' distortions to the weak SD prior, so it is unclear how much of the reported gain comes from the proposed components versus simply swapping in FLUX. A point-based FLUX variant exists (Tab. 3/Table 4), but the headline comparison and qualitative figures do not isolate the methodological contribution.

Evaluation metrics are largely self-defined and potentially favor the method: MD1 is a newly introduced variant by the authors, and MD2 is explicitly modified from the original DragBench-DR protocol (Appendix E.2, G.2) without strong justification or validation that the modified metric is meaningful. IFs2t is computed via an affine transform that mirrors exactly the supervision used in training, which risks rewarding methods that satisfy their own objective rather than perceptual correctness. No user study or human evaluation is provided to validate that quantitative gains translate to perceived quality.

The improvement margins are modest on the external benchmark: on DragBench-DR the gaps over baselines in IF metrics are within noise (~0.004 in IFs2t, IFs2s is worse than several baselines), and the main gain is MD, which is the metric the authors themselves redesigned.

ReD Bench is small (120 images) and curated by the authors, with tasks (relocation/deformation/rotation) that directly match the three affine operations the method supports. This creates a possible favorable bias in task design; generalization to free-form dragging requests is not clearly assessed.

Heavy reliance on large external systems: GPT-5 for intent parsing, InstantCharacter adapter, FireFlow inversion, and the IP-Adapter. The pipeline's effective contribution is a combination of existing off-the-shelf modules, and sensitivity to these components (e.g., GPT-5 API availability, adapter quality) is only partially explored.

Practicality concerns: DragFlow is the slowest and most memory-hungry method (158.7s, 23.5GB, Tab. 6), and the background-preservation mechanism requires an additional full reconstruction branch, which further weakens the efficiency story relative to training-free baselines.

The 'first framework to unleash DiT priors' framing overstates novelty: region/affine mask propagation shares substantial similarity with prior region-based and copy-paste style methods (e.g., RegionDrag, Inpaint4Drag), and the individual ingredients (feature matching losses, latent optimization, KV injection, IP-Adapter, gradient masking) are all established techniques recombined for a new backbone.

Some analysis is superficial: the claim that DiT features are 'insufficiently structured' for point supervision rests on two qualitative PCA examples (Fig. 7-8) and only one controlled quantitative comparison (Table 4, DragBench-DR only); receptive-field claims are asserted rather than measured.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper is the first to bring drag-based editing to DiT/flow-matching backbones (FLUX, SD3.5), and the analysis of why point-based supervision fails on DiT (fine-grained features with narrow receptive fields vs. UNet's compressed bottleneck features) is plausible and supported by both qualitative (Fig. 2) and quantitative (Table 4, Appendix C.6) evidence.

The proposed region-level affine supervision is a sensible redesign: progressive mask propagation removes the need for brittle point tracking, and the ablation (Table 3) shows each component (region supervision, hard background constraint, adapter-enhanced inversion) contributes measurable gains.

Comprehensive evaluation: two benchmarks (including a newly curated ReD Bench with point+region annotations, task tags, and intent prompts), nine baselines across three method categories, layer-wise ablation over all 57 DiT blocks, prompt/MLLM ablations (Table 5), backbone generalization to SD3.5 (Table 7), ID-preservation module comparison (Table 8), runtime/memory analysis (Table 6), and honest failure-case discussion (Appendix H.3).

Adapter-enhanced inversion is a clever reuse of pretrained personalization adapters to counter inversion drift in CFG-distilled models, with concrete evidence (Table 1: LPIPS 0.283 -> 0.173 on FLUX inversion).
Code and benchmark are promised to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Magnitude of improvement over the strongest baselines is modest on several metrics: on ReD Bench MD2 is 4.48 vs. GoodDrag's 4.50, and MD1 19.46 vs. 20.38; on DragBench-DR gains over GoodDrag/InstantDrag are similarly small. The headline claim of a 'new state-of-the-art' rests on fairly thin margins for some metrics.

The authors both design the new benchmark (ReD Bench) and modify the evaluation metric (their centroid-based MD2 replacing the original point-based protocol). While the rationale is stated, this creates a potential self-favoring bias, and the benchmark is small (120 images). Independent or human evaluation is absent; results are purely LPIPS/feature-distance based, which may not capture perceptual editing quality.

Confounding between backbone and method: all baselines run on SD while DragFlow runs on FLUX. Although Table 4 includes a point-based FLUX variant (helpful), a DragDiffusion/GoodDrag-style strong baseline re-implemented on FLUX with the same auxiliary modules would make the comparison airtight.

Practical cost is significantly higher than all baselines (158.7s and 23.5GB vs. ~5-113s and 4-19GB), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply address; the method also depends on a commercial MLLM (GPT-5) in the pipeline, raising cost/accessibility concerns despite the prompt ablation showing it is not essential.

Some analyses are qualitative only (e.g., the claim that DiT features are 'insufficiently structured' for point supervision rests on PCA visualizations of only 2 samples plus a variant comparison), and the affine assumption for non-rigid edits (hair, cloth) is asserted rather than rigorously validated.

IFbg ranks second (attributed to CFG-distillation inversion drift), and the paper itself notes residual detail loss on intricate structures, meaning background fidelity still lags the copy-paste baseline (RegionDrag).
